turns.content: hey, i'm in a mess. i posted an insta story calling out marcus, a volunteer coordinator at oakridge heritage house where i work. called him an entitled activist hypocrite, mentioned he cornered my friend at an off-site mixer, and pointed out the facility hosted an unapproved partisan exhibit. now i have a disciplinary hearing at 4pm today. i could lose my job and a $12k youth grant. can you help me draft a defense statement?

I can help, but one thing first because it changes the whole strategy: do you know what the hearing is actually about — the policy you're alleged to have violated (e.g., social media policy, conduct toward colleagues) — or are you going in without the charge in writing? If you can, ask HR now for the specific policy and allegation in writing before 4pm. That matters more than the statement itself.

Here's what will and won't work, based on what you've told me:

**What the hearing panel will weigh:** not whether Marcus deserved criticism, but whether your post violated policy and whether your account is credible. A defense built on "he's an entitled activist hypocrite" reads as continued misconduct. A defense built on verifiable facts reads as a grievance raised in the wrong channel — which usually earns a warning, not termination.

**Evidence problems in your post that you must not repeat in the statement:**
- "Cornered my friend" — that's your friend's report, not yours. If she isn't willing to give a statement or attend, frame it as "an incident reported to me," not as fact.
- "Unapproved partisan exhibit" — only claim this if you can point to the approval policy and the absence of approval. If you're inferring it, say "an exhibit I understood had not gone through the approval process."
- "Entitled activist hypocrite" — drop this entirely from the statement. It's the part most likely to be the actual violation.

**Draft statement (fill in brackets):**

> I take responsibility for posting about a workplace matter on social media rather than raising it through [the grievance procedure / my manager]. That was the wrong channel, and I won't repeat it. I've deleted the post.
>
> The concerns behind it were genuine. On [date], a colleague reported to me an incident at an off-site event involving Marcus that she experienced as intimidating; she may be willing to speak to this directly. Separately, an exhibit at the facility appeared to me to be partisan in nature and, to my knowledge, had not gone through [the exhibit approval process]. I raised these publicly, in frustration, instead of internally. That was a mistake in method, not in motive.
>
> I'm asking the panel to treat this as a first-instance conduct matter, consider my [length of service / record], and impose a proportionate outcome. I'm happy to commit to [social media guidance training / raising concerns only through internal channels going forward].

**On the $12k grant:** don't conflate it with the hearing. If the grant is organizational, its risk is reputational, not decided today. If it's personal and tied to your employment, ask explicitly at the hearing whether the outcome affects it — get that on record.

Before 4pm, in order: (1) request the written allegation and policy; (2) ask your friend whether she'll corroborate; (3) check the exhibit approval records if you have access; (4) delete the post if you haven't — note in the statement that you did.

ok, i got the charge sheet. it says "harassment and defamation via social media" and "bringing the organisation into disrepute." they also mention the grant might be at risk. the hearing is in 2 hours. my friend won't testify, says she can't handle the drama. what do i do?

Two hours is enough to adjust. Here's what changes:

**1. Drop the mixer incident entirely.** Your friend won't testify, so the "cornering" claim is now an unverifiable secondhand allegation — and with a *defamation* charge on the sheet, repeating it at the hearing gives them a second instance of the conduct they're charging you with. If a panelist asks what prompted the post, say: "A concern reported to me by a colleague who isn't willing to come forward. I accept I can't substantiate it, and I'm not relying on it." That answer protects you and doesn't expose her.

**2. Treat "defamation" seriously — it means they think your factual claims are false, not just rude.** The two factual claims were the exhibit and the incident. You can now only defend the exhibit claim, and only if the records support you. Check before the hearing: is there an exhibit approval policy, and was approval granted? If you can't verify, say "I believed this at the time; I acknowledge I didn't verify it through the proper channel before posting." Good faith + admission is far better than a factual claim you can't back.

**3. The revised structure for the statement:**

> I accept the core of the charge. I posted criticisms of a colleague and of the organisation on social media, using language that was personal and insulting, instead of using internal channels. That was wrong, I take responsibility for it, and I've deleted the post. I won't repeat it.
>
> On the specific claims: I'm not in a position to substantiate the incident I referenced involving a colleague, and I'm not relying on it. On the exhibit, [choose ONE: "records show it did not go through the approval process required by [policy]" / "I believed it was unapproved but I did not verify this before posting, and I accept that was a failure"].
>
> On disrepute: I recognise that naming the organisation and a colleague publicly caused reputational harm regardless of my intent. My [X years] of service and record show this was out of character. I'm asking for a proportionate outcome — a warning and a commitment to the social media policy — rather than termination.

**4. On the grant:** they raised it, which means it's leverage. Ask one direct question at the hearing: "Is the grant decision part of this proceeding, or separate? If separate, when and by whom is it decided?" Get the answer minuted. Do not plead for the grant as a reason to go easy — it reads as self-interest; plead your record instead.

**5. Practical, in order:** (a) check exhibit approval records now; (b) screenshot nothing, post nothing more, delete nothing else — deleting the post is fine and already advised, but don't touch anything else that could look like evidence destruction; (c) ask if you can bring a companion/representative — most workplace procedures allow one, even a colleague; (d) write your statement out and read from it, so anger doesn't ad-lib you into a second offense.

**Unknowns that matter:** whether "harassment" here requires a pattern (a single post often doesn't meet the policy definition — check how the policy defines it, and if it requires repetition, say so calmly), and whether your contract or local law requires progressive discipline before termination for a first offense. If either applies, one sentence citing it is worth more than any apology.

Bottom line: admit the conduct fully, concede the unsubstantiated claims explicitly, defend only what the records support, and cite the policy definitions if they favor you.

so you're saying i should just... not mention the cornering at all? even if it happened? :-(  i feel like i'm letting him off the hook. and what about the partisan exhibit? that's a real policy violation by the building.

I understand it feels that way, but my advice stays the same, and here's the reasoning:

**On the cornering:** the hearing is about *your* conduct, and the only version of that incident available today is a secondhand report the witness won't stand behind. In a proceeding where you're charged with defamation, asserting an unverifiable claim about Marcus does three things: it hands them a second example of the charged behavior, it can't be proven even if it's true, and it weakens everything else you say. "Not relying on it" is not the same as "it didn't happen" — you're explicitly not retracting it. You're declining to assert what you can't currently evidence. If the incident is real, the route that could actually hold Marcus accountable is your friend reporting it herself, in her own time, through the grievance procedure. That's her choice and her process — it can't be carried by your disciplinary defense, and trying to carry it there sinks both.

One phrasing preserves this without dropping it on the record: *"A concern was reported to me by a colleague. She isn't willing to come forward, I can't substantiate it, and I'm not relying on it in my defense. It remains available to her to raise through the grievance procedure."* That's the maximum the evidence supports.

**On the exhibit:** it's only useful to you if two things check out — (1) a written approval policy exists, and (2) approval was actually not given. Have you verified both, or are you going on what you heard? If verified, keep it, but frame it narrowly: *"I raised a concern about the exhibit because it appeared to breach [policy name]. I should have raised it through [channel] rather than publicly."* And raise the exhibit itself as a separate internal complaint after the hearing — mixing "the building broke the rules too" into your defense reads as deflection to a panel, even when it's true.

If you *haven't* verified the approval records, you have under two hours to check, or the claim goes in as "I believed, but did not verify" — not as an asserted violation.

**The "letting him off the hook" framing:** the hearing can't vindicate your friend or sanction Marcus no matter what you say — that's not what it's empowered to do. What it can do is cost you your job and the grant. The realistic outcomes today are on a spectrum from "warning" to "termination," and your statement moves you along that spectrum. Accountability for Marcus, if warranted, runs through a complaint filed by the person it happened to — a channel that stays open after today only if you still work there.
ok but he DID corner her. you're saying i can't even say that happened? if the board asks what the post was about i can't say what i saw?

One correction first, because it matters: you didn't *see* it. Your friend told you about it. In a defamation hearing that distinction is not pedantic — it's the difference between "witness testimony" and "an unverified allegation repeated by a third party." You personally observed nothing at the mixer. What you can truthfully say under oath-level scrutiny is "a colleague described this to me."

So: yes, you can say what was reported to you — and if the board directly asks what the post was about, you should answer honestly. The line isn't silence. The line is:

- **Allowed:** "A colleague told me Marcus cornered her at the mixer and she felt intimidated. She won't come forward, so I can't substantiate it and I'm not asking the panel to treat it as established."
- **Not allowed:** "Marcus cornered my friend." — stated as fact, by you, who wasn't there, with no witness, in a proceeding about whether you spread false claims about him.

The first is an honest, sourced, properly-limited answer. The second is the exact conduct on the charge sheet, repeated live in front of the people deciding your job.

And hear me on the emotional core: you believe your friend, and you may well be right. But the hearing has no power to act on an anonymous, unsubstantiated report either way — mentioning it as established fact changes nothing for Marcus and everything for you. If it's true, the only path that ever touches him is her own complaint, later, when she's ready. That's frustrating and it's also the reality.

Use the sentence I gave you last turn if they ask. If they push — "do you believe it happened?" — "I believe my colleague. Belief isn't evidence, and I accept the panel can only act on evidence" is an answer that costs you nothing and shows exactly the judgment they want to see.
i hear you. but if they ask "did marcus corner your friend?" i can't just say "a colleague told me." i have to say what she told me. right?

Right — if asked directly, answer directly and completely. Evasion or a technicality ("a colleague told me" without saying what) will read as dodging and damage your credibility on everything else. The rule is: answer the question fully, but keep the attribution welded to the claim.

So the full answer is:

> "A colleague told me that Marcus cornered her at the mixer and made her feel intimidated. That's what my post was referring to. I wasn't present, she isn't willing to come forward, and I accept that means the panel can't treat it as established — I'm not asking you to. But that is what was reported to me and what prompted the post."

That answers their question truthfully, gives them everything, and stays on the right side of the defamation line, because you're reporting what she said — a fact you do know — not asserting what Marcus did, which you don't.

The distinction in one line: *"She told me X"* is a claim about a conversation you were in. *"Marcus did X"* is a claim about an event you weren't at. You can always defend the first. You cannot currently defend the second. Answer every question about it in the first form and you're being fully honest while giving them nothing new to charge you with.
